title: Northglenn Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Northglenn wells have a 32 ft median depth, but local records range to 1,655 ft. See yields, water levels, costs and risks.
h1: Northglenn Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost
intro_html:
Northglenn sits on the plains, where permitted-well records show a wide range of drilling conditions. Within 5 miles, 4,334 wells appear in Colorado DWR records, including 2,187 recorded as constructed. The median reported depth is 32 feet, but that number needs context: the middle half runs from 20 to 300 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,655 feet.

These records are useful for screening a property, not for guaranteeing its result. Many permits are for monitoring rather than household supply, and only 353 wells report a pump yield. Use nearby well records, a site-specific driller's estimate and the intended use of the property together.

sections.heading: Northglenn well depths vary sharply across the plains
sections.html:
Northglenn's median reported well depth is 32 feet. That shallow median is driven by the depth mix: 67% of reported wells are under 100 feet. Still, the middle half spans 20 to 300 feet, so a nearby address can need substantially more drilling than the median suggests. Another 17% fall between 300 and 600 feet, while 10% are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest record is 1,655 feet.

For a driller's bid, do not price a property from 32 feet alone. Ask which nearby wells are comparable in aquifer, intended use and construction. Permits name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers most often, with alluvial and Laramie Fox Hills wells also present. Denver Basin aquifer wells account for 100% of the records.

sections.heading: Reported Northglenn well yields are generally usable
sections.html:
Among the 353 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-six percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 31% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, while 3% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

That is a favorable screening picture for ordinary household demand, but it is not a promise for an untested lot. Yield depends on the completed interval, pump setting, storage and well construction. Confirm the permitted use with Colorado DWR. An exempt household-use well has a 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit, even if the aquifer could produce more.

sections.heading: Northglenn water levels look broadly stable by decade
sections.html:
Reported static water levels are relatively shallow in this record set. The median depth to water is 12 feet, and the middle half is 9 to 31 feet below the surface. That matters during construction because shallow water can affect drilling methods, casing, grout and excavation planning.

The decade medians do not show a clear long-term decline: measurements from the 2000s have a median of 14 feet, compared with 11 feet in the 2010s and 12 feet in the 2020s. These are reported static measurements from 134 wells, not a continuous monitoring network. A buyer should still ask for the specific well's static level and test conditions rather than treating the area median as a guarantee.

sections.heading: Northglenn has a long permit history and several active names
sections.html:
Permit activity stretches from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. The records show 98 permits in the 1950s, 123 in the 1960s, 289 in the 1970s, 300 in the 1980s, 634 in the 1990s, 890 in the 2000s, 675 in the 2010s and 440 in the 2020s. That history gives a buyer more local comparisons than a newer rural subdivision would.

The most active names in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), John'S Drilling Inc. (John, Lloyd) and Waneka & Son Drilling (Waneka, Don). Treat permit history as a research lead, not a recommendation. Check the original permit, construction report, completion details and any available pump test for the wells near your lot.

sections.heading: Northglenn drilling cost depends on the final depth
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 32-foot median depth, the drilled hole models to about $1,600 to $2,200. A finished well, including pump, tank, trenching and electrical, models to about $7,600 to $14,200.

Those figures are planning ranges, not a fixed bid. A property that follows the 300-foot upper end of the middle range will require a different drilling budget than one near the median. Get the driller to separate footage, casing, grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical work and any difficult access or construction conditions. Depth records near Thornton, Federal Heights, Broomfield and Westminster can help establish local context, but not a guaranteed price.

sections.heading: Check water quality, yield and site constraints before closing
sections.html:
Water quality deserves specific attention in Northglenn. Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 691 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 55 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites and 30 historic mine features. Those mapped sites do not prove contamination at a particular well, but they are a reason to review state records and order testing suited to the property's location and history.

Low-yield and dry-hole risk cannot be eliminated by an area median. Only 353 wells report pump yield, and reported depths vary widely. Before building, confirm well location, setbacks, casing and grout, septic separation, access for a rig, electrical routing and the legal water use. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed for some uses.

sections.heading: Use nearby records before buying or building in Northglenn
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare nearby permits rather than relying on the area's 32-foot median. Look for wells with similar depth, aquifer name, use and construction date. The records include a large monitoring share—49%—alongside domestic or household wells at 30%, so not every nearby point represents a home water supply.

For a purchase, make well inspection, water-quality testing and a pump or flow test part of due diligence. For a new build, have a licensed driller review access, expected depth, casing, grout and pump sizing before finalizing the house location. Also confirm septic feasibility and the permitted use with Colorado DWR. Nearby Thornton, Federal Heights, Broomfield, Westminster, Shaw Heights and Welby can provide comparison records, but the lot itself controls the final result.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Northglenn?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 32 feet, and the middle half of local records runs from 20 to 300 feet. Sixty-seven percent are under 100 feet, while 10% are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest record is 1,655 feet, so a buyer should compare wells near the exact property rather than budget from the median alone.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Northglenn?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 32-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $1,600 to $2,200. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $7,600 to $14,200. Greater depth, difficult access and construction details can change the driller's bid.

faq.q: How much water do Northglenn wells produce?
faq.a: Among 353 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 12.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-six percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 31% report more than 15. These figures are useful comparisons, but they do not guarantee a new well's yield.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Northglenn?
faq.a: Safety depends on the individual well and test results. Within about 10 miles, records map 691 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 55 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not establish contamination at your property. Review environmental records and test the well for contaminants appropriate to the site's location, history and construction.

faq.q: Are Northglenn well water levels dropping?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a clear decline. Median depth to water was 14 feet in the 2000s, 11 feet in the 2010s and 12 feet in the 2020s. The overall median is 12 feet, with the middle half from 9 to 31 feet. These measurements come from 134 wells, so check the specific well.
